processing: Mature leaves are scrubbed of the fuzz on their undersides, dried and crushed, and in many products roasted.
harvest_season: Leaves of an evergreen tree, not tied to a prized picking; older, mature leaves are preferred, ideally two years or more.
appearance_dry: Crushed brown-green to dark brown pieces of tough leaf.
appearance_liquor: Clear red-brown, deeper in roasted versions.
taste_profile: Mild and easy, close to a soft oolong or roasted tea, with a little earth and little aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Best simmered: a common home ratio is 20 g of crushed leaf to 1 litre of water for about 20 minutes on low heat. Remove the fuzz from fresh leaves first.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, as loose leaf or tea bags, all year, often labelled by prefecture. Roasted and unroasted versions taste different, so check which you are getting.
description:
Biwa-cha is an infusion of loquat leaves, from the same tree that gives the small orange fruit. It is an old home remedy in Japan that has become a shelf product, with no true tea in it.

Home makers want older leaves, scrub the fuzz off the underside, bake them until crisp and crush them. The fuzz step matters because those hairs are irritating. Commercial packs are usually roasted, which is what gives the cup its familiar brown colour.

The result is a gentle cup somewhere near oolong or hojicha, with little to dislike. Because the leaf is tough it wants a long simmer rather than a short steep. Some people add milk, and it takes to that well.

Ignore the bigger promises on the box. Research on loquat leaf compounds exists, but effects in people are not established. Look for origin on the label and buy for an easy evening drink.
history: Loquat has been grown in Japan for a long time, and its leaves have been used in folk medicine, either dried for tea or applied directly to the skin. Some producers in Kagoshima trace the tea back to the 14th century, but that is a seller's claim with no independent support, and the real date of the first cup remains unknown.
